steps.tx: **Damage control resuscitation** is early blood products, limited crystalloid, permissive hypotension until bleeding is controlled, and rapid surgery or angioembolisation. It does not apply unchanged to traumatic brain injury. Prioritising balanced haemostatic resuscitation prevents the lethal triad of hypothermia, profound metabolic acidosis, and trauma-induced coagulopathy.

steps.tx: **PROPPR** compared a 1:1:1 ratio of plasma, platelets, and red cells with 1:1:2. More patients achieved **haemostasis** with 1:1:1. Mortality at 24 hours and 30 days was not significantly different. Reconstituting whole blood physiology with equal component ratios achieved superior anatomical haemostasis and significantly reduced exsanguination deaths in the first 24 hours.

rows: 1 unit plasma : 1 pool platelets : 1 unit PRBC
1 unit plasma : 1 pool platelets : 2 units PRBC
Lower early haemostasis rate; equal overall 30-day mortality
Initiate immediate 1:1:1 activation in major exsanguination

steps.tx: **CRASH-2** showed that **tranexamic acid** 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours, reduced death from bleeding when given within 3 hours of injury. Giving it after 3 hours was associated with harm. Inhibiting plasminogen activation halts hyperfibrinolysis, but delayed administration exacerbates endothelial thrombosis and increases late mortality.

Inhibiting plasminogen activation halts hyperfibrinolysis, but delayed administration exacerbates endothelial thrombosis and increases late mortality.

left.title: Timely administration within 3 hours
points: Loading dose 1 g IV over 10 minutes
Maintenance infusion 1 g IV over 8 hours
Significant relative reduction in death from bleeding

right.title: Delayed administration after 3 hours
points: Paradoxical increase in bleeding and all-cause mortality
Strict contraindication outside the 3-hour post-injury window

steps.tx: **Permissive hypotension** targets a systolic pressure around 80 to 90 mmHg until surgical control, and only if there is no traumatic brain injury. With brain injury the pressure is kept higher, commonly a systolic pressure of at least 110 mmHg. Keeping blood pressure modest avoids popping the haemostatic clot and minimizes dilution before surgical clamping.

rows: Prevents clot disruption and dilutional coagulopathy
Systolic BP at least 110 mmHg (MAP 80 mmHg)
Maintains cerebral perfusion pressure to prevent secondary ischaemia
Restricts intravenous fluid volume to blood products

steps.tx: **Viscoelastic tests**, **TEG** or **ROTEM**, guide product replacement when they are available. A low **fibrinogen**, below about 150 to 200 mg/dL, is replaced with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate. Rapid whole-blood dynamic clot analysis detects hypofibrinogenaemia, platelet dysfunction, and hyperfibrinolysis within minutes, allowing goal-directed rather than empiric component replacement.

left.title: Viscoelastic metrics (ROTEM/TEG)
points: Clotting time (CT/R) guides fresh frozen plasma
Alpha angle and clot firmness (A10/MCF) guide fibrinogen

right.title: Targeted fibrinogen replacement
points: Fibrinogen is the first coagulation factor to become depleted
Maintain serum level strictly above 150 to 200 mg/dL
Administer 10 units cryoprecipitate or 2 to 4 g fibrinogen concentrate

steps.tx: **Citrate** in blood products binds calcium. **Ionised calcium** is checked and replaced during massive transfusion. Hypocalcaemia worsens coagulopathy and cardiac function. Preservative citrate prevents storage clotting, but rapid infusion of multiple units overwhelms hepatic metabolism, precipitating severe ionised hypocalcaemia that paralyzes coagulation factor complexes and causes ventricular arrhythmias.

Preservative citrate prevents storage clotting, but rapid infusion of multiple units overwhelms hepatic metabolism, precipitating severe ionised hypocalcaemia that paralyzes coagulation factor complexes and causes ventricular arrhythmias.

rows: Hypocalcaemia directly halts tenase and prothrombinase
1 to 2 g calcium chloride or gluconate IV
Administer for every 4 units of blood products transfused

steps.tx: **Prothrombin complex concentrate** reverses **warfarin** faster than plasma and does so with less volume. It does not replace fibrinogen and it does not reverse a platelet problem. Four-factor PCC contains concentrated vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X, rapidly normalizing the international normalized ratio within fifteen minutes without risking circulatory volume overload.

left.title: Four-factor PCC reversal
points: Contains concentrated factors II, VII, IX, and X
Restores normal INR in under 15 to 30 minutes
Small volume infusion eliminates TACO risk

right.title: Clinical limitations
points: Does not contain therapeutic fibrinogen or platelets
Requires concurrent intravenous vitamin K for sustained synthesis
Ineffective for primary platelet consumption coagulopathy

steps.tx: **Crystalloid resuscitation** of haemorrhage dilutes clotting factors and does not carry oxygen. It is a bridge only until blood arrives. Infusing large volumes of saline causes hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, exacerbates hypothermia, disrupts vascular endothelial glycocalyx architecture, and accelerates exsanguination in uncontrolled trauma.
